items.title: How to Write a Romance Built on Character, Not Beats
items.summary: There are no real shortcuts to writing something good, especially since there are so many ways to attack story. The closest you can probably get if you're writing in a specific genre is to look at that genre's story tropes and just copy the steps. I'm thinking in this case specifically of Lifetime and Hallmark movies, and how they always hit the same beats. Romance actually is a great example of a genre in which the beats are both reliable and expected by the audience. But story consultant Brian Williamson, who runs the channel Plot Luck, has a slightly different approach. In a recent video, he points out that you can hit every convention the romance genre asks for and still leave an audience cold, because, as he said, "love does not care about your beat sheet." If viewers don't believe in the romance and the characters, then why would they keep watching at all? His recommendation is to grow the relationship out of the two people in it, and he builds the whole thing using the acronym HEART (hold, exchange, awaken, risk, transform). Let's look at each step. - YouTube www.youtube.com Hold (What They Believe About Love) Before your couple meets on the page, Brian said, each of them already believes something about love, and it's not just "love language" or type. "What has this person decided somewhere deep down in their bones that love actually is?" Maybe a character watched a marriage fall apart and decided love never lasts. Maybe a long run of rejection convinced them it isn't in the cards. In (500) Days of Summer, Tom writes greeting cards and believes that he has a single soulmate somewhere out there. Meanwhile, Summer isn't looking for anything serious and sees a relationship as passing. The mismatch is what causes all the drama between them. Brian says the writer's first move is to have each character finish two phrases. First: "Love is ___." Then: "If I let myself love someone, then ___." items.title: The Real Skill Behind Getting a Movie Made
items.summary: Making a movie is brutal. It's hard. We know. But the lead-up to the green light might even be worse. Before you get to hire actors or buy props, you often have to sit across from someone holding the money and talk them into parting with it. It's a skill that has almost nothing to do with filmmaking. You have to be a performer yourself. StudioBinder's new video on how films get greenlit is basically a clinic on pitching, assembled from writers and directors who have managed to get good at it. As screenwriter Jeremy Slater puts it, "It doesn't matter how good you are on the page if you don't get hired for the job in the first place. And that's a problem, because most writers are introverted weirdos who spend way too much time alone. Suddenly we're shoved into a room and asked to be passionate and funny and charismatic, and for a lot of us, that's an utterly foreign skill set. It's f***ing terrifying" (via SYFY). If that's you, here's what the people who've cracked it do differently. - YouTube www.youtube.com Find the Right Room Before anything else, figure out who you're talking to. Do your dang research and know the platform you're pitching. A studio executive and an indie financier want different things, and if you're just starting out in the industry, your idea should read as manageable and low-risk, not a hundred-million-dollar gamble. For example, Jordan Peele approached Get Out as a producer first, mining what worked without a big budget. Neill Blomkamp says in the video (speaking during San Diego Comic Con): “I suppose if you're James Cameron or you're Peter Jackson, then having a lot of money probably is pretty cool because you can have a lot of money and do what you want. But if you're not them, you have to kind of start off with films that are, you know, either smaller and you can do what you want, or bigger and you can't do what you want.” Knowing your buyer influences everything that follows. items.title: 10 Overlooked Movies of 1991
items.summary: 1991 was a huge year for movies, so it makes sense that there are a lot of overlooked titles left on the table. Who could pay attention to every movie coming out in between all-timer titles like The Silence of the Lambs, Beauty and the Beast, Boyz n the Hood, Terminator 2: Judgment Day, Home Alone, and Thelma & Louise? We’re only human. We simply don’t have the bandwidth. However, as these movies all celebrate their 35th anniversary, let’s take a look at 10 underappreciated 1991 gems that deserve more attention. 10. Sleeping with the Enemy This Julia Roberts thriller is the lowest on the list because it was actually a huge hit in 1991, ultimately becoming the seventh highest-grossing movie at the domestic box office that year. However, over time, it has been overshadowed by the other 1990s Julia Roberts classics that came both before (Pretty Woman) and after it (My Best Friend’s Wedding, Runaway Bride, Notting Hill, 2000’s Erin Brockovich). Regardless of its reputation relative to her overall filmography, Sleeping with the Enemy is a winner, blending small town romance with slasher-thriller tropes in a delicious way that many a Lifetime movie has tried to replicate over the years. 9. The People Under the Stairs The People Under the Stairs is a Wes Craven classic that deserves to be on the Mount Rushmore of his filmography alongside A Nightmare on Elm Street, Scream, and The Last House on the Left. In addition to boasting trenchant subtext about white landlords abusing tenants of color, the movie is a wild thrill ride that features two exquisitely twisted villain performances from Twin Peaks alumni Wendy Robie and Everett McGill. 8. Poison Poison, which is the debut feature of Todd Haynes (Carol, May December), interweaves three stories adapted from Jean Genet novels. items.title: The 1927 Film That Ended Hollywood’s Silent Era
items.summary: Thanks to the past several decades of commercialized cinema, it’s easy to forget that they were at one time completely devoid of dialogue. They relied on inserted cue cards or music to communicate entire storylines. But one film in 1927 changed everything: The Jazz Singer. The Silent Film Golden Age The 1910s and 20s were booming decades for silent cinema. The films were often cheap to make, save for the larger D.W. Griffith-style epics due to lack of modern technology, and theatre-like staging, reducing the need for extensive editing. From a consumer standpoint, cinema was still seen as a cheaper alternative to live theater, which drove more mass amounts of consumerism. Key movie stars like Lillian Gish began to emerge during the silent film era as recognizable faces that would draw the public in for new releases. Gish starred in dozens of films in the silent era, and while she still played a key role in iconic films like The Night of the Hunter post-1927, her career, like many others', was severely jeopardized by the invention of sound. Having fully relied on only their faces for performance, the transition into delivering dialogue often proved too much for silent film stars. The Release of ‘The Jazz Singer’ ‘The Jazz Singer’Credit: Warner Bros. The film itself follows a young Jewish man struggling with his dreams to pursue a career as a Jazz performer to the reluctance of his traditional family. The film isn’t entirely a “talkie” per se. Al Jolson’s character has individual music numbers that are performed in the “talkie” style, but a large portion of the film still remains silent. This made the presentation of the film largely difficult on premiere night. The respective projectionist had to manage fifteen different film reels for the film’s 89-minute-long runtime alongside separate reels and sound discs for the main character’s musical numbers. items.title: 5 Best Paced Movies of All Time
items.summary: Pacing can simultaneously be any movie’s secret weapon, as well as its most potent inadequacy. You could be doing everything right at the most pristine level technically, but if you start to bore your audience with a 90-minute runtime, you’re in trouble. But you could also make 150-180 minutes feel like 90 if you do everything right. Here are some of the best-paced movies of all time. 1. Star Wars: Episode IV - A New Hope Before all of the episodic mumbo jumbo, there was just one film: Star Wars. Coming in at a pre-credit runtime of exactly 120 minutes, the film is a master of pace, because it’s firstly a master of structure. The original film perfected the length of a traditional hero's journey structure, and made sure that each beat of the formula took exactly as much time as it needed to be completed. So much so that to this day, the traditional length for blockbusters of this style remains close to the exact two-hour mark. One could certainly make the argument that the film’s sequel, The Empire Strikes Back, somehow perfects its sense of pace even more than the original due to the expansions of the lore and technical prowess, but for the sake of the pacing of this article (see what I did there?), we’ll move on. 2. Raiders of the Lost Ark ‘Raiders of the Lost Ark’Credit: Walt Disney Studios Another Lucas/Spielberg production, the first installment in the now iconic Indiana Jones franchise revolutionized film pacing in a bit of a different way. The film follows a similar structure to the hero’s journey formula, except it bypasses the prologue and origin story-esque elements. Indiana Jones is already a seasoned archaeologist in the opening scene, making for one of the most iconic action scenes of all time right from the jump. The film takes a break for a few minutes afterwards to actually set up the story, but once the brief exposition scene in Barnett College is complete, the film doesn’t stop moving.
